title: Why did 40,000 people queue for stockings?
teaches: Rayon (viscose) as regenerated cellulose; what a polymer is; Carothers and nylon at DuPont (1935, on sale 15 May 1940); nylon at war; polyester, acrylic and spandex; why synthetics are now about two thirds of the world's fibre and why that is not simply a loss

blocks.text: In June 1946, about 40,000 people queued along a mile of a Pittsburgh street for a chance to buy one of 13,000 pairs of nylon stockings. Fights broke out, and newspapers across the United States reported similar scenes in other cities that year, which they called the nylon riots. Nylon stockings had gone on sale only six years earlier, and then almost disappeared for the war, when the government took nearly all nylon for military use.

Every fibre in this course so far, from flax and wool to silk and cotton, was grown by a plant or an animal. Nylon was the first fibre made entirely by chemists from small molecules. Today synthetic fibres make up about two thirds of all the fibre the world produces. In this lesson we look at how chemists learned to make fibres, what the new ones do better and worse than natural ones, and how they took over.

The first step was not a new molecule. Lesson 2 described cotton and flax as made of **cellulose**, the long-chain molecule that forms the walls of plant cells. Wood is mostly cellulose too, but its fibres are short and stiff. In the 1880s the French chemist Hilaire de Chardonnet dissolved cellulose and pushed the solution through tiny holes to make long, shiny filaments, which he showed at the Paris exhibition of 1889 as artificial silk. His version was dangerously flammable.

In 1892 three British chemists, Charles Cross, Edward Bevan and Clayton Beadle, patented the **viscose** process. Wood pulp is treated with caustic soda and carbon disulphide until it forms a thick, honey-coloured liquid, the viscose. This is pumped through a **spinneret**, a metal cap pierced with fine holes, into a bath of acid, where the cellulose sets again as filaments. The British silk firm Courtaulds began making viscose yarn in 1905, and it was sold widely as artificial silk until American makers named it **rayon** in 1924.

blocks.caption: Three ways to get the long-chain molecules a fibre needs.

blocks.text: Rayon is therefore a **regenerated** fibre: its molecules are natural cellulose, but the fibre is made in a factory, and its length, thickness and shine are set by the spinneret. It took dye well, draped like silk and cost far less, and by the 1930s it was used for dresses, linings and stockings. Making it had a hidden cost. Carbon disulphide is a poison that damages the nervous system, and many workers in viscose plants suffered depression, psychosis and nerve damage for decades before factories controlled their exposure.

Why do some molecules make fibres and others do not? In the 1920s the German chemist Hermann Staudinger argued that substances such as cellulose, rubber and silk are made of **polymers**: very long molecules built from thousands of small, identical units joined end to end, like beads on a string. Many chemists doubted him at first, but by the 1930s the idea was accepted. A fibre is a bundle of such chains lying roughly side by side. The longer the chains and the more neatly they line up, the stronger the fibre.

Staudinger's idea suggested that chemists might build such chains themselves, from small molecules that join on to each other when heated with the right partners. Cellulose (cotton, flax, rayon), keratin (wool) and fibroin (silk) are natural polymers. The fibres in the rest of this lesson are polymers that do not occur in nature.

In 1928 the American chemical company DuPont hired Wallace Carothers, a young chemist from Harvard, to lead a laboratory doing basic research on polymers. His group made many new long-chain molecules. In February 1935 they made a **polyamide**, a polymer of two building blocks that alternate along the chain, which could be melted, drawn out into a filament and stretched until its chains lined up, giving a fibre stronger than silk and very elastic. DuPont called it **nylon**.

DuPont aimed nylon at the most valuable use for silk in the United States: women's stockings, which were knitted (lesson 4) from silk imported almost entirely from Japan (lesson 22). It announced nylon in 1938, and the first nylon product to go on sale was a toothbrush. Nylon stockings went on sale across the United States on 15 May 1940, and many shops sold out on the first day. Carothers did not see it: he had died in 1937.

In July 1941 the United States froze Japanese assets, and silk imports stopped. After the United States entered the war that December, the government took nearly all nylon production for parachutes, tow ropes for gliders, tyre cords and other military uses, and stockings disappeared from the shops. Women drew a line up the back of their legs with eyebrow pencil to imitate a stocking seam. When nylon stockings returned in 1945 and 1946, demand was far greater than supply, which is how a queue of 40,000 formed in Pittsburgh.

In 1941, in Manchester, John Whinfield and James Dickson of the Calico Printers' Association made **polyester** from chemicals derived from oil. It was sold in Britain as Terylene and in the United States as Dacron from the early 1950s. Polyester can be made as a continuous filament or cut into short lengths and spun like cotton, and it blends well with cotton and wool. Shirts and suits of polyester blends could be washed and worn without ironing, and in the 1960s and 1970s polyester went into almost everything. Other synthetics followed, including acrylic, a soft wool substitute, from 1950, and spandex, sold as Lycra, a very stretchy fibre for sportswear and underwear, from 1959.

blocks.caption: World fibre production by type, 1950 to 2023. Rounded figures from industry estimates; 'made from wood' means rayon and other regenerated cellulose.

blocks.text: Synthetic fibre passed cotton in the 1990s, and polyester alone is now more than half of all fibre made. Most of it is spun in China, from chemicals made from oil and natural gas.

Synthetics are often described as a cheap, inferior replacement for natural fibre. The picture is mixed. Polyester and nylon are much stronger than cotton for their weight, they keep their shape, they dry quickly and they resist rot and moths. They are cheap because they are made in vast continuous plants instead of grown, so their price does not depend on harvests, land or the weather, and they use far less land and water than cotton. Many things are hard to make well without them: climbing ropes, seat belts, sportswear, fleece, tights and most outdoor clothing.

Their weaknesses come from the same chemistry. Polyester absorbs almost no water: under standard conditions it holds about 0.4 percent of its weight in moisture, against about 8 percent for cotton and 15 percent for wool, so it feels clammy when you sweat and tends to hold body odour. Synthetics are made from fossil fuels, they shed tiny fibres when washed, and they do not rot away, which lesson 26 takes up. Blends of cotton and polyester are especially hard to recycle, because the two fibres have to be separated first.

**Where it went next.** The polymers developed for fibres became plastics. Nylon is used for gears, zips and machine parts. The polyester of a shirt, polyethylene terephthalate or PET, is the same material as most plastic drinks bottles, and recycled bottles are now a large source of the polyester used in clothing.

items.ask: Why is rayon called a regenerated fibre rather than a synthetic one?
choices: Its molecules are natural cellulose from wood, dissolved and reformed into a fibre
It is grown by a plant
It is made from oil
It is a blend of silk and cotton
items.why: Rayon starts from cellulose that a tree made. The factory changes the fibre's shape, not its molecules.

choices: A very long molecule built from many small units joined in a chain
A mixture of two fibres
A dye that binds to cloth
A machine that spins filaments
items.why: Staudinger's idea was that fibres such as cellulose and silk are long chains of repeating units, which chemists could then try to build.

items.ask: Why did DuPont aim nylon first at women's stockings?
choices: Stockings were the largest use of silk in the US, and that silk came almost entirely from Japan
Nylon could not be knitted into anything else
Stockings were the cheapest product to make
Cotton stockings had been banned
items.why: Replacing imported silk in its most valuable use gave nylon a large, ready market.

items.ask: Why were there queues and fights for nylon stockings in 1946?
choices: The war had taken almost all nylon for military use, so demand had built up while supply was still short
Nylon had just been invented
Silk stockings had become cheaper
Stockings were rationed by law in 1946
items.why: From 1942 nylon went to parachutes, ropes and tyres. When stockings returned, years of pent-up demand met limited output.

items.ask: Polyester holds about 0.4 percent of its weight in moisture, cotton about 8 percent. What follows?
choices: Polyester dries fast but feels clammy against sweaty skin
Polyester is weaker than cotton
Cotton dries faster than polyester
Polyester cannot be dyed
items.why: A fibre that absorbs little water dries quickly, but it cannot soak up sweat the way cotton or wool does.

summary: **Rayon came first.** From the 1890s, cellulose from wood pulp was dissolved and spun into filaments as artificial silk.
**Fibres are polymers.** Long chains of repeating units, lined up side by side, give a fibre its strength.
**Nylon was built from scratch.** Carothers's group at DuPont made it in 1935, and stockings went on sale on 15 May 1940.
**War took the nylon.** With Japanese silk cut off, nylon went to parachutes and ropes, which is why stockings were scarce until 1946.
**Polyester took over.** From the 1950s it made wash-and-wear clothing, and it is now more than half of all fibre made.
**Synthetics are about two thirds of fibre today.** They passed cotton in the 1990s.
**They are strong, cheap and quick-drying.** They also feel clammy, come from fossil fuels, shed microfibres and are hard to recycle in blends.
**Fibre chemistry made plastics.** The polyester in a shirt is the same PET as a drinks bottle.
